title: Cornstarch goo on a shaking speaker grows fingers that rise and wriggle

cover.alt: A pale, thick cornstarch paste sitting in the cone of a small black loudspeaker, with two lumpy fingers sticking up from it.

body: Mix cornstarch with a little water and you get a **shear-thickening** fluid, sometimes called oobleck: stir it slowly and it flows, but hit it hard and it resists like a solid. Under strong, fast shaking a layer of such a mixture can hold shapes no ordinary liquid could, including holes that stay open and fingers that stand up. [Physicists at the University of Texas](https://arxiv.org/abs/nlin/0311026) described them in 2004. Why the shapes last is still debated: the first explanation was shear thickening, and later work points to the way dense mixtures stay stiff for a while after being stressed.

slides.alt: A pale paste fills the cone of a small black speaker. Lumpy fingers push up out of it, stretch, wobble, sag back and rise again in new places.
slides.caption: Aboard the space station, astronaut Don Pettit put cornstarch goo on a computer speaker. As it vibrates, fingers of goo rise, wobble and sink back.
slides.credit: NASA Johnson · Public domain · excerpt, cropped
slides.music: “Android Sock Hop” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.heading: Same goo, two ways to push it

left.label: Slow and gentle
left.text: A spoon or finger sinks in, and the mixture flows like a thick liquid.

right.label: Fast and hard
right.text: The mixture stiffens and resists the force, acting for a moment like a solid.

slides.heading: Why it stiffens
slides.text: Forcing the mixture to move fast knocks the starch grains out of their resting places, and they crowd into clumps called hydroclusters. Like logs jamming in a river, the clumps lock up and the goo stops flowing freely.

slides.label: how hard a layer of cornstarch goo had to be shaken for holes poked in it to stay open
slides.text: In the 2004 experiments, the holes' rims began sprouting fingers once the shaking passed about 17 times the pull of gravity.

slides.question: Which of these has been tested with shear-thickening fluid in it?
slides.explanation: In one study, Kevlar soaked in a shear-thickening fluid did better than Kevlar alone: the fluid spreads a sudden blow over a wider area.
